title: Nearby places
summary: Geospatial indexing with geohash or quadtrees.
prompt: Design “find places near me”: given a location and radius, return nearby businesses (restaurants, shops) ranked by distance and rating. Business owners can add and edit listings.

requirements: Functional: search by location, radius and optional category; view a business; owners create and update listings.
Non-functional: search in ~100 ms at p99; read-heavy; edits may take minutes to appear.
estimation: 200M businesses × ~1 KB of metadata ≈ 200 GB; the geo index needs only (id, lat, lng, category) ≈ tens of bytes each, so ~10 GB.
100M daily users × 5 searches ≈ 500M a day ≈ 6,000/s average.
Writes (edits) are tiny by comparison: thousands per day.
api: GET /businesses/{id}; POST and PUT /businesses for owners.
data: businesses(id, name, lat, lng, category, rating, …) as the source of truth.
geo_index(geohash prefix → business ids) or a quadtree held in memory by the search service.
Geohash precision 6 cells are roughly 1.2 km × 0.6 km, a reasonable bucket for city searches.
design: Search service: compute the geohash of the user location at a precision matching the radius, query that cell and its 8 neighbours, then filter by exact distance and rank.
Writes go to the business DB; a change stream updates the geo index within minutes.
Business details are cached; the read-only geo index is replicated for read throughput.
deepDives: Why neighbours: a point near a cell edge has close businesses in the adjacent cell, so always search the 3×3 block.
Geohash vs quadtree: geohash prefixes map well onto ordinary key-value or B-tree indexes; a quadtree adapts cell size to density (dense cities split more).
Ranking blends distance with rating and relevance; apply exact haversine distance only to the small candidate set.
bottlenecks: Dense areas return too many candidates: use finer precision or cap and rank.
Sparse areas return too few: widen the radius step by step.
Hot cells (city centres): cache popular cell results briefly.
tradeoffs: A periodically rebuilt index is simpler but staler than real-time updates; listings rarely move.
Fixed geohash cells are simple; adaptive quadtrees balance load at the cost of more complex rebuilds.
A specialised geo database is less work but less control than an in-memory index.

rubric.text: Chose a spatial index (geohash, quadtree or similar) and explained the lookup.
Searched neighbouring cells to handle boundary cases.
Filtered candidates by exact distance and ranked them.
Separated the read-optimised index from the write path.
Estimated index size and query rate.
Planned replication or sharding of the index by region.
